Amazed
uh-MAYZD
v. (past part.)
From maze, a bewilderment or labyrinth; the Old English sense is to stupefy, to confound. Webster 1828: astonished; confounded with fear, surprise or wonder. In the Gospels it is the standing reaction of the crowds to Christ, and once it is used of Christ Himself in Gethsemane.

Biblical Definition

Amazed is Mark’s word above all, and it describes something stronger than admiration. At Capernaum, after the unclean spirit came out, they were all amazed, insomuch that they questioned among themselves, saying, What thing is this? what new doctrine is this? for with authority commandeth he even the unclean spirits, and they do obey him (Mark 1:27). The amazement is not at a miracle in the abstract but at authority; the crowd is trying to place a category of person they have never met. Luke records the same after the palsied man rose: they were all amazed, and they glorified God, and were filled with fear, saying, We have seen strange things to day (Luke 5:26). Amazement in the Gospels is regularly joined to fear, and it is not the same thing as faith — the same crowds that were amazed also cried, Crucify him. The most solemn use is Gethsemane: he taketh with him Peter and James and John, and began to be sore amazed, and to be very heavy (Mark 14:33). The Greek is strong, and the King James translators did not soften it. The Son of God, going to bear the wrath He had known from eternity was coming, was struck with a horror His humanity felt to the full.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines AMAZED as astonished, confounded with fear, surprise or wonder; and AMAZEMENT as astonishment, confusion, perplexity arising from terror or wonder. The older English kept the element of terror the modern word has lost.

expand to see more

AMAZED, pp. — Astonished; confounded with fear, surprise or admiration.

AMAZEMENT, n. — Astonishment; confusion; perplexity arising from a sudden impression of terror, or from an object of wonder.

The root is maze, a state of bewilderment, as one lost in a labyrinth; the original force is disorientation, not delight.

Webster notes that the word formerly implied terror more strongly than in his own day — a drift that has continued, so that amazing is now nearly a compliment.

This drift matters for reading Mark 14:33: sore amazed in 1611 English meant something close to struck with horror.

Key Scripture

Mark 1:27 — "And they were all amazed, insomuch that they questioned among themselves, saying, What thing is this? what new doctrine is this? for with authority commandeth he even the unclean spirits, and they do obey him."

Mark 10:32 — "And they were in the way going up to Jerusalem; and Jesus went before them: and they were amazed; and as they followed, they were afraid. And he took again the twelve, and began to tell them what things should happen unto him,"

Luke 5:26 — "And they were all amazed, and they glorified God, and were filled with fear, saying, We have seen strange things to day."

Mark 14:33 — "And he taketh with him Peter and James and John, and began to be sore amazed, and to be very heavy;"

Acts 3:10 — "And they knew that it was he which sat for alms at the Beautiful gate of the temple: and they were filled with wonder and amazement at that which had happened unto him."

Modern Corruption

Modern worship aims at amazement and calls it encounter, but the Gospels are careful to distinguish amazement from faith: the amazed crowds are the same crowds that afterward wanted Him dead.

expand to see more

Mark records amazement constantly and conversion rarely. The crowds are astonished at His doctrine, astonished at His authority, astonished beyond measure at the healing of the deaf man, and the same city that thronged Him is the one where the multitude is persuaded to ask for Barabbas. Amazement is a response of the affections to power, and fallen affections respond to power without submitting to it. This is worth saying plainly wherever corporate worship is designed to produce a peak emotional experience and that experience is then treated as evidence of the Spirit’s work. The regulative principle asks a different question of a service: not whether the people were moved, but whether God was worshipped as He commanded. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.

Mark 14:33 must not be softened, and the classical doctrine is what keeps it from being distorted in either direction. The Chalcedonian confession holds two natures in one Person, without confusion and without division. The horror in Gethsemane is real and is felt in the human nature the Son assumed; the divine nature is impassible and does not suffer change. This is not a technicality. It is what allows a Christian to say both that his Saviour truly knows dread — sore amazed, very heavy, sweating as it were great drops of blood — and that the God on whom he leans is not Himself shaken. Take away either half and the comfort collapses.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek existemi (G1839), to stand out of oneself, to be beside oneself; thambeo (G2284) and ekthambeo (G1568), to be struck with awe or terror — the latter used of Christ in Gethsemane.

expand to see more

Greek thambeo (G2284) — to be astounded, struck with awe; they were all amazed (Mark 1:27).

Greek ekthambeo (G1568) — to be greatly amazed, struck with terror; sore amazed (Mark 14:33).

Greek existemi (G1839) — to displace, to be beside oneself; they were all amazed (Luke 5:26).

Greek ekstasis (G1611) — amazement, a standing outside oneself; filled with wonder and amazement (Acts 3:10).

Greek ademoneo (G85) — to be in distress or heaviness; the companion word in Mark 14:33, very heavy.

Usage

"What new doctrine is this? (Mark 1:27) — amazement at authority, not merely at power."

"They were amazed; and as they followed, they were afraid (Mark 10:32) — the disciples on the road to Jerusalem."

"Began to be sore amazed, and to be very heavy (Mark 14:33) — the word the translators would not soften."
